title: Inheritance in practice
hook: fixed shares for family, and up to a third by will

segments.voice: Yesterday, children's rights, and your line: fair to each. A father walked his son to the Prophet, and the gift went back. Did you catch yourself handing out more to one than another? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-three.

Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas is lying sick in Mecca, sure he is about to die. He is a man of some wealth, and he has one daughter to inherit from him. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ comes to visit, and Sa'd asks him straight out: may I give all my wealth away in charity? It sounds like a beautiful question. The Prophet says no. Then half? No. Then a third? And the Prophet answers: a third, and a third is a lot. Tradition says Sa'd recovered. But that bedside bargain became a line in Islamic law. Today is about what happens to what you leave behind.
screen: `SA'D ON HIS SICKBED.` → `ALL? NO. HALF? NO.` → `A THIRD, AND A THIRD IS A LOT.`

segments.voice: Islamic inheritance works in two layers. The first layer is fixed by the Qur'an itself. In surah four, God names the shares: what children receive, what parents receive, what a husband or wife receives. The verses call them an ordinance from God, and the jurists built a whole science around them, called fara'id, the obligatory shares. You don't choose these. When a Muslim dies, the family's portions are already written. The second layer is yours. Before the shares are divided, the debts are paid and the will is carried out, and the will can reach up to a third of what is left. That third is where a person can remember a friend, a cause, a mosque, a stranger who was kind. Then a limit on the will itself: a report in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi says there is no bequest to an heir. The ones who already have a share from the Qur'an can't be given extra by will. The third is for people the shares don't reach. Now back to Sa'd's sickbed, because the Prophet gave a reason. In Sahih al-Bukhari, he tells Sa'd that leaving his heirs well off is better than leaving them dependent, holding out their hands to people. So the limit isn't a limit on generosity. It is generosity pointed in two directions at once: to your family, through the shares, and to the wider world, through the third. A family may sit down with a scholar to work out the exact shares, and the schools disagree on some of the rarer cases. But the shape holds: the debts, the third, then the shares.
screen: `LAYER ONE: SHARES FIXED IN SURAH FOUR.` · `LAYER TWO: A WILL, UP TO A THIRD.` · `NO BEQUEST TO AN HEIR.` · `LEAVE THEM WELL OFF, NOT DEPENDENT.`

segments.voice: The practice is a very simple will, written only in your head for now. Start with what you owe: anyone you'd want paid back, any promise you'd want kept. Then think about your third. Not the money, the people. Who, outside your family, would you want to remember? A teacher, a neighbor, a place that fed you once? Hold one name. If it feels right, you can write it down later, or talk to someone about making it real. The bell holds the time.
Inheritance in practice. Fixed shares for the family from the Qur'an, and up to a third by will for those the shares don't reach. Today's word.

Your line: a third by will. Today, think of one person outside your family you'd want to remember, and tell them something kind while you're both here. Tomorrow, the marketplace. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: When a Muslim dies, debts are paid first, then any will of up to a third is carried out, and the rest is divided among family members by the shares set out in surah four, often with a scholar's help.

original.note: Arabic: the obligatory shares; the science of dividing an inheritance.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Muslim's will decides who gets everything.
what it means: the Qur'an fixes the family's shares; a will can reach only up to a third.
what a scholar hears: 'ilm al-fara'id, Sa'd's report in Bukhari, and 'no bequest to an heir' in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 2742; Sahih Muslim 1628 (Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and the third)
Sunan Abi Dawud 2870; Jami' at-Tirmidhi 2120 (no bequest to an heir)

notes: Sa'd's report: confirm details (in Mecca, during the farewell pilgrimage in some versions; one daughter; all/half/third; 'a third, and a third is a lot'; heirs rich rather than dependent). 'Recovered and lived on' is in some versions of the report; confirm.
Qur'an 4:11–12 paraphrased; 'an ordinance from God' paraphrases the verse's own language; confirm.
Order debts, then will, then shares: from 4:11–12 ('after any bequest... or debt') and jurists' ordering of debts first; confirm.
'No bequest to an heir' unless other heirs consent (some schools); not mentioned in voice; Keeper may want it.
The schools disagreeing on rarer cases is stated without counts; confirm phrasing.
